questions.q: When should you research a realistic salary range for a first BI developer role?
options: Before you're deep into any interview process, using at least two independent sources for your actual metro area
Only after an offer has already been extended
You don't need to — the employer will always name a fair number first
Only after you've accepted the job, to check if you were paid fairly
questions.explain: Negotiation preparation starts weeks before an offer. Building a realistic range ahead of time, from multiple sources, is what lets you answer expectations questions and evaluate an offer with confidence.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend avoiding naming a number first whenever possible?
options: Whoever names a number first gives away information — a lower number caps the offer, and a high number risks getting screened out too early
It's illegal to name a number first in most states
Employers always increase whatever number a candidate names
Salary numbers should never be discussed at any point in a hiring process
questions.explain: Naming a number first anchors the rest of the negotiation to it. Letting the employer name a number first, or answering with a range instead of a figure, protects you from capping your own offer.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to answer "what are your salary expectations" if you're pushed for an answer on an early call?
options: Answer with your researched range, not a single invented number
Refuse to answer the question at all
Give the highest number you can imagine, regardless of research
Give a number lower than you want so you seem easy to work with
questions.explain: Answering with a researched range keeps you from committing to a single number that might be lower than what the employer would have actually paid, while still giving them something concrete to work with.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does a respectful counter-offer include?
options: A thank-you for the offer, a researched range instead of a demand, a reason grounded in market data, and a collaborative tone rather than an ultimatum
A threat to accept a competing offer that doesn't actually exist
A refusal to discuss the offer until it is doubled
A demand for an exact figure with no room for discussion
questions.explain: The sample script in this lesson thanks the employer, cites researched market numbers, asks whether there's room to move, and stays open to either outcome — it's a request, not a demand.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say to look at more than just the base salary number before accepting or countering an offer?
options: Because the full package — signing bonus, PTO, review timeline, remote flexibility, and other benefits — can make a lower base worth more overall
Because base salary is the only part of an offer that matters
Because bonuses and benefits are never part of a real offer
Because negotiating anything besides base salary is not allowed
questions.explain: Total compensation includes more than the headline base number. A slightly lower base with strong PTO and a fast path to a raise can be worth more than a higher base with neither.
